transcription.tex: \textbf{Lines and planes}\par 1. Write vector and Cartesian equations of lines.\par 2. Describe a plane using two directions or a normal vector.\par 3. Use scalar products to find angles.
\textbf{Geometry in three dimensions}\par 4. Find intersections and distinguish skew lines.\par 5. Calculate shortest distances.\par 6. Reflect points and lines in planes.

slides.title: Vector equation of a straight line in 3D

transcription.tex: A vector equation describes every point on a straight line.\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}3\\0\\-2\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]Find the points for \(\lambda=0,1,2,-1\).

The first vector locates a fixed point. The second gives the direction.\par Changing \(\lambda\) moves along the line in either direction.\par The direction vector is non-zero.\[\mathbf r=\mathbf a+\lambda\mathbf b\]

slides.title: Cartesian form of equation of straight line

transcription.tex: For a line \(\mathbf r=\mathbf a+\lambda\mathbf b\):\[x=a_1+\lambda b_1,\ y=a_2+\lambda b_2,\ z=a_3+\lambda b_3\]
This form assumes all three direction components are non-zero. If \(b_2=0\), write \(y=a_2\) separately; do not divide by zero.\par A Cartesian equation has no free parameter.

transcription.tex: The plane $\Pi$ has vector equation $\mathbf r=3\mathbf i-2\mathbf j+\mathbf k+\lambda (-2\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+5\mathbf k)+\mu (4\mathbf i+2\mathbf j-3\mathbf k)$. transcription.tex: $AB$ is a diameter of a circle centred at the origin $O$, and $P$ is a point on the circumference of the circle. By considering the position vectors of $A$, $B$ and $P$, prove that $AP$ is perpendicular to $BP$.\par Problem-solving\par This is a vector proof of the fact that the angle in a semi-circle is $90^\circ$.

Proof Write \(\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a\), \(\overrightarrow{OB}=-\mathbf a\), \(\overrightarrow{OP}=\mathbf p\).\[\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\overrightarrow{BP}=(\mathbf p-\mathbf a)\cdot(\mathbf p+\mathbf a)\]\[=|\mathbf p|^2-|\mathbf a|^2=0\]The two radii have equal length, so the angle is a right angle.

transcription.tex: Challenge\par 1 Using the definition $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\cos \theta $, prove that $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf a$.\par 2 The diagram shows arbitrary vectors $\mathbf a$, $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$, and the vector $\mathbf b+\mathbf c$.
\[\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\cos\theta=\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf a\]

a Show that:\par i $\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b+\mathbf c)=|\mathbf a|\times PQ$\par ii $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=|\mathbf a|\times PR$\par iii $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c=|\mathbf a|\times RQ$\par b Hence prove that $\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b+\mathbf c)=\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b+\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c$.

\[\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b+\mathbf c)=|\mathbf a|\,PQ\]\[\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=|\mathbf a|\,PR\]\[\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c=|\mathbf a|\,RQ\]Each follows by resolving the second vector along \(\mathbf a\).
\[PQ=PR+RQ\]\[\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b+\mathbf c)=|\mathbf a|(PR+RQ)\]\[=\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b+\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c\]

shapes.alt: Regular tetrahedron. The faces ABD and ACD share edge AD. BC is the hidden edge.

transcription.tex: Proof Let \(E\) be the midpoint of \(AD\). Both \(EB\) and \(EC\) are perpendicular to \(AD\).\[E=(1/2,0,1/2)\]\[EB=(-1/2,1,1/2)\]\[EC=(1/2,1,-1/2)\]\[\cos\angle BEC=\frac{1/2}{\sqrt{3/2}\sqrt{3/2}}=\frac13\]Regularity gives the same angle at every edge.

Decision \[FA=(0,8,-18),\quad FC=(-2,6,-15)\]\[\cos\theta=\frac{318}{\sqrt{388}\sqrt{265}}\]\[\theta\approx7.4^\circ<15^\circ\]The condition fails for these two ropes, so the pole is not stable.
